summary:
We are honored to present our web-based platform, designed to help local farmers make smarter and more sustainable crop rotation decisions.
By combining farmer-provided information about their land with NASA's open Earth observation data, we developed a solution that transforms environmental data into practical agricultural insights and tailored crop rotation recommendations.
We believe that the use of our platform can contribute to a more efficient, resilient, and sustainable agricultural future.
details:
DAWRA Project Description and Architecture

1. Project Overview

Our project, DAWRA, is a multilingual agricultural web application designed to help local farmers make better decisions about crop rotation, irrigation, and resource management.

The application combines information provided by the farmer with environmental data from NASA POWER. It then analyzes the selected field and produces practical recommendations adapted to the local agricultural context.

DAWRA is designed as a decision-support tool. It does not replace an agricultural expert, but it helps farmers understand their field conditions and make more informed decisions.

2. How the Project Works

The user begins by selecting a field location manually on an interactive map. The application obtains the field’s coordinates and automatically determines the nearest agricultural region.

The farmer then enters information such as:

  • Soil type
  • Current crop
  • Previous crops
  • Field size
  • Irrigation availability
  • Water conditions
  • Crop preferences
  • Other field characteristics

DAWRA combines this information with:

  • NASA POWER climate and environmental data
  • Local agricultural region profiles
  • Crop characteristics
  • Water-management rules
  • Crop-rotation rules
  • Agricultural calculation formulas

The application then calculates different indicators, evaluates possible risks, and generates crop-rotation recommendations.

The final result may include:

  • Climate indicators
  • Water requirements
  • Irrigation guidance
  • Soil and field risks
  • Crop-rotation options
  • Rotation scores
  • Crop sequences
  • Explanation of the recommendation
  • Data limitations and warnings

The system is currently based on deterministic calculations and predefined agricultural rules. It does not use an AI or machine-learning model to generate the recommendations.

3. Main Benefits

DAWRA provides several important benefits for farmers and agricultural advisors.

Better decision-making

The application transforms several types of information into a clear recommendation, helping farmers make decisions based on data rather than guesswork.

Water-resource management

Water requirements and irrigation guidance help farmers understand how much water their crops may require and how water availability affects their decisions.

Improved crop rotation

The system proposes crop rotations that consider soil, climate, water availability, and crop compatibility.

Risk identification

DAWRA highlights risks related to climate, soil, water stress, irrigation, and crop selection.

Local adaptation

The analysis uses regional agricultural profiles and the selected field coordinates, making the result more relevant than a general recommendation.

Accessibility

The application is designed to be simple and responsive. It supports English, French, and Arabic/Darija so that it can be used by people with different language backgrounds.

Practical results

The farmer can save, print, or share the results through WhatsApp. The application also allows saved history to be cleared and provides a logout option.

4. Intended Impact

The main goal of DAWRA is to support more sustainable and climate-aware agriculture.

The project is intended to:

  • Help farmers manage water more efficiently.
  • Encourage better crop rotation.
  • Protect soil quality.
  • Reduce agricultural risks.
  • Improve productivity through better planning.
  • Make environmental data easier to understand.
  • Support farmers facing climate variability.
  • Provide useful guidance to farmers who may not have easy access to agricultural experts.

In the long term, DAWRA could contribute to more resilient local agriculture by helping farmers adapt their practices to environmental conditions and available resources.

5. Technical Architecture

DAWRA uses a lightweight web architecture.

User Interface
|
v
Map and Farmer Input Layer
|
v
Application State and Event Logic
|
v
NASA POWER Data Layer
|
v
Agricultural Analysis Engine
|
v
Indicators and Recommendations
|
v
Local Storage, Printing, and WhatsApp Sharing

Frontend

The frontend is built with:

  • HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript

The frontend provides:

  • Navigation
  • Forms
  • Map interaction
  • Field selection
  • Language selection
  • Analysis display
  • Risk indicators
  • Recommendations
  • Account controls
  • Print and WhatsApp sharing

The application works as a single-page web application without requiring a framework such as React or Angular.

Backend and server

The project uses Node.js with a lightweight server.

The server is responsible for:

  • Serving the frontend files
  • Hosting the web application
  • Providing local development access
  • Supporting deployment

The main application analysis runs in the browser.

Analysis engine

The analysis engine combines the following:

  • Farmer inputs
  • Selected coordinates
  • Regional agricultural profiles
  • NASA POWER environmental data
  • Crop-rotation rules
  • Water calculations
  • Risk thresholds

It generates consistent, explainable results based on the provided data.

Data persistence

The application uses browser local storage instead of a remote database.

It can store:

  • User profile data
  • Saved analyses
  • Crop history
  • Selected language

The user can clear the saved history at any time.

Progressive Web App

DAWRA includes Progressive Web App functionality through:

  • manifest.json
  • Service-worker support
  • Offline asset caching
  • Responsive design

This allows the application to behave more like an installable mobile application.

6. External Data and Services

NASA POWER

NASA POWER is the main external source used for environmental and climate information.

The application uses NASA data to support:

  • Climate analysis
  • Water calculations
  • Environmental indicators
  • Irrigation recommendations

If the external request is unavailable, the application can use cached or fallback data.

Map services

External map libraries and map tiles are used to display the map and allow manual field selection.

The map is used for visualization and coordinates. It does not directly generate agricultural recommendations.

7. Tools and Software Used

Our team used several tools during the development, organization, testing, and deployment of the project.

Programming technologies

  • HTML for the structure of the application.
  • CSS for the visual design, layout, and responsive behavior.
  • JavaScript for the user interface, map interaction, calculations, localization, and recommendation logic.
  • Node.js for the local web server and application hosting.
  • Git for version control.
  • GitHub for repository hosting and project history.

Netlify

We used Netlify as a web deployment and hosting platform.

It supports the publication of the web application so that users can access it online without running the project locally.

Google Drive

We used Google Drive for:

  • Sharing project documents
  • Storing presentation materials
  • Organizing team files
  • Collaborating on written content
  • Keeping project resources accessible to team members

Claude Pro

We used Claude Pro as an assistance and productivity tool during development.

It helped with:

  • Brainstorming ideas
  • Improving written explanations
  • Reviewing possible project structures
  • Generating suggestions
  • Discussing user experience and presentation choices

Claude Pro was used as a development assistant, not as the agricultural analysis engine inside DAWRA.

GitHub Copilot

We used GitHub Copilot to support software development.

It helped with:

  • Writing and improving code
  • Understanding existing code
  • Debugging
  • Refactoring
  • Creating interface logic
  • Improving translations
  • Testing development ideas
  • Reviewing implementation details

The final agricultural recommendations are still produced by the application’s own deterministic rules and calculations.

NASA POWER

NASA POWER was used as the main environmental data source for climate-related analysis.

Map libraries and browser tools

We used map libraries and browser developer tools to:

  • Display the map
  • Select coordinates
  • Test user interaction
  • Debug the interface
  • Verify application behavior

8. Creativity of the Project

DAWRA is creative because it combines different information sources into a simple and practical agricultural decision process.

Instead of showing raw climate values, the application interprets them and connects them to:

  • Soil conditions
  • Crop choices
  • Irrigation availability
  • Regional characteristics
  • Crop rotation
  • Water management

The project also makes the result interactive. The user selects a real field location and receives a recommendation related to that location.

Other creative aspects include:

  • Automatic regional assignment
  • Multilingual support
  • Clear explanations of risks
  • Crop-rotation scoring
  • WhatsApp report sharing
  • Offline-friendly behavior
  • Local storage for saved analyses
  • Plain-language agricultural guidance

The central creative concept is:

Turn complex environmental data into a simple and practical decision for a farmer.

9. Factors Considered by the Team

During development, we considered several technical, agricultural, and social factors.

Local agricultural needs

The project focuses on the needs of local farmers and regional agricultural conditions.

Water scarcity

Water availability was treated as a major factor because efficient water use is essential for sustainable agriculture.

Climate change

Climate variability and changing environmental conditions were considered when designing the indicators and recommendations.

Soil protection

Crop rotation was selected as an important solution for maintaining soil quality and reducing repeated pressure on the same soil resources.

Ease of use

The application was designed to be simple enough for users who may not have advanced technical knowledge.

Language and accessibility

English, French, and Arabic/Darija support were included to make the application more accessible.

Privacy

The application does not request browser GPS location. The user selects the field manually, and saved data is stored locally in the browser.

Reliability

The project includes fallback behavior for situations where NASA POWER data or network access is temporarily unavailable.

Transparency

The recommendations are based on visible calculations and rules, making it easier for users to understand how the result was produced.

Practical use

We considered how farmers might use the result outside the application. This is why the project includes printing and WhatsApp sharing.

Technical limitations

The current version does not include:

  • A remote user-account system
  • Cloud synchronization
  • Agricultural sensors
  • Satellite imagery analysis
  • A machine-learning recommendation model
  • Full property-boundary mapping

These limitations were considered so that the current project would remain realistic, understandable, and implementable.

10. Project Impact Summary

DAWRA aims to make agricultural planning more accessible, data-informed, and sustainable.

By combining farmer knowledge, local agricultural information, and NASA environmental data, the project helps transform complex information into practical recommendations. It encourages farmers to use water more efficiently, select more suitable crop rotations, understand risks, and adapt their decisions to local environmental conditions.

Final Summary

DAWRA is a multilingual agricultural decision-support web application that uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Node.js, NASA POWER data, map services, and rule-based agricultural calculations to help local farmers choose crop-rotation plans and manage their resources more intelligently. The project was developed with the support of Netlify, Google Drive, Claude Pro, and GitHub Copilot. Its intended impact is to promote sustainable agriculture, improve water management, protect soil, and support farmers in making clear and informed decisions.
